references.authors: Salmon CP, Knize MG, Felton JS
references.title: Effects of marinating on heterocyclic amine carcinogen formation in grilled chicken.
references.finding: A brown sugar/olive oil/cider vinegar/garlic/mustard/lemon marinade cut PhIP in grilled chicken by 92-99% and total HCAs from 56 to 1.7 ng/g (20 min) and 330 to 44 ng/g (40 min), but MeIQx rose >10-fold at 30-40 min cooking.

references.authors: Smith JS, Ameri F, Gadgil P
references.title: Effect of marinades on the formation of heterocyclic amines in grilled beef steaks.
references.finding: Commercial herb/spice marinades applied for 1 h cut total HCAs in beef steaks grilled at 204 °C by 57-88%; rosemary-type polyphenols (carnosic acid, carnosol, rosmarinic acid) were abundant in the best marinade.

references.authors: Felton JS, Fultz E, Dolbeare FA, et al.
references.title: Effect of microwave pretreatment on heterocyclic aromatic amine mutagens/carcinogens in fried beef patties.
references.finding: Microwaving beef patties for 1-3 min before frying (and discarding the juice) removed up to 30% of HCA precursors and cut the four main HCAs 3- to 9-fold and mutagenicity up to 95%.

references.authors: Salmon CP, Knize MG, Panteleakos FN, et al.
references.title: Minimization of heterocyclic amines and thermal inactivation of Escherichia coli in fried ground beef.
references.finding: Turning beef patties every minute at lower pan temperatures greatly reduced HCAs versus a single turn, while still reaching the 70 °C internal temperature that fully inactivated E. coli, with little or no extra cooking time.

references.authors: Sinha R, Chow WH, Kulldorff M, et al.
references.title: Well-done, grilled red meat increases the risk of colorectal adenomas.
references.finding: Each 10 g/day of well-done/very-well-done red meat was associated with 29% higher odds of colorectal adenoma (OR 1.29) versus 10% (NS) for rare/medium; grilled red meat OR 1.26 per 10 g/day.

references.authors: Martínez Góngora V, Matthes KL, Castaño PR, et al.
references.title: Dietary Heterocyclic Amine Intake and Colorectal Adenoma Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest intake of PhIP (OR 1.20), MeIQx (1.20), DiMeIQx (1.16), benzo(a)pyrene (1.15) and meat mutagenicity (1.22) were associated with colorectal adenoma, with dose-response for PhIP and MeIQx.

references.authors: Chiavarini M, Bertarelli G, Minelli L, et al.
references.title: Dietary Intake of Meat Cooking-Related Mutagens (HCAs) and Risk of Colorectal Adenoma and Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Meat-cooking mutagens were associated with colorectal adenoma (PhIP OR 1.20) and cancer (MeIQx OR 1.14, DiMeIQx 1.12, mutagenicity 1.12), with high heterogeneity in some analyses.

references.authors: Viegas O, Yebra-Pimentel I, Martínez-Carballo E, et al.
references.title: Effect of beer marinades on formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in charcoal-grilled pork.
references.finding: Marinating pork in black beer cut the EFSA PAH8 marker group in charcoal-grilled meat by 53% (non-alcoholic Pilsner 25%, Pilsner 13%), in line with each marinade's radical-scavenging activity.

references.authors: Gibis M
references.title: Effect of oil marinades with garlic, onion, and lemon juice on the formation of heterocyclic aromatic amines in fried beef patties.
references.finding: In oil marinades for fried beef patties, garlic and onion (not lemon juice) dose-dependently reduced MeIQx by up to ~70%; HCA levels were low overall (MeIQx 0.38-1.22 ng/g).

references.authors: Cross AJ, Sinha R
references.title: Meat-related mutagens/carcinogens in the etiology of colorectal cancer.
references.finding: High-temperature cooking of meat forms HCAs and PAHs, and endogenous N-nitroso compound formation rises with red meat intake; reviews their role in colorectal cancer.

references.authors: Bouvard V, Loomis D, Guyton KZ, et al.
references.title: Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat.
references.finding: IARC Monograph 114 working group classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A), noting that high-temperature cooking generates HCAs and PAHs.

references.authors: Ollberding NJ, Wilkens LR, Henderson BE, et al.
references.title: Meat consumption, heterocyclic amines and colorectal cancer risk: the Multiethnic Cohort Study.
references.finding: No association between total or specific HCA intake (RR Q5 vs Q1 0.90, 0.76-1.05), red meat or processed meat and colorectal cancer; a modest effect could not be ruled out.

references.authors: Sugimura T, Wakabayashi K, Nakagama H, et al.
references.title: Heterocyclic amines: Mutagens/carcinogens produced during cooking of meat and fish.
references.finding: HCAs are potent mutagens and rodent carcinogens, but their content in ordinary dishes is low and not sufficient by itself to explain human cancer; reducing exposure is still recommended.

references.authors: Cross AJ, Ferrucci LM, Risch A, et al.
references.title: A large prospective study of meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk: an investigation of potential mechanisms underlying this association.
references.finding: Red and processed meat were associated with colorectal cancer; heme iron, nitrate/nitrite and HCAs (MeIQx HR 1.19, DiMeIQx HR 1.17 top vs bottom quintile) were candidate mechanisms.

references.authors: Duedahl-Olesen L, Ionas AC
references.title: Formation and mitigation of PAHs in barbecued meat - a review.
references.finding: PAH mitigation in barbecued meat: remove visible char, minimise fat dripping onto the heat source, use acidic marinades and leaner cuts; exposure estimation is hampered by varied practices.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM)
references.title: Scientific Opinion on acrylamide in food
references.finding: EFSA CONTAM Panel: mean adult dietary acrylamide exposure 0.4-0.9 µg/kg bw/day (95th percentile 0.6-2.0); BMDL10 0.17 mg/kg bw/day for tumours in mice; margins of exposure indicate a concern for neoplastic effects, while neurotoxicity and reproductive effects are not a concern at current exposure.

references.authors: Benford D, Bignami M, Chipman JK, et al.
references.title: Assessment of the genotoxicity of acrylamide.
references.finding: EFSA statement: newer studies confirm acrylamide and glycidamide are genotoxic (glycidamide DNA adducts also seen in humans), with additional ROS-mediated and non-genotoxic effects; the 2015 margin-of-exposure approach and conclusions still stand.

references.authors: Pelucchi C, Bosetti C, Galeone C, et al.
references.title: Dietary acrylamide and cancer risk: an updated meta-analysis.
references.finding: Dietary acrylamide was not related to most common cancers; borderline kidney cancer RR 1.20 (1.00-1.45), and in never-smokers endometrial RR 1.23 and ovarian RR 1.39 (CI crossing 1).

references.authors: Adani G, Filippini T, Wise LA, et al.
references.title: Dietary Intake of Acrylamide and Risk of Breast, Endometrial, and Ovarian Cancers: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-analysis.
references.finding: Higher acrylamide intake was associated with slightly higher ovarian and endometrial cancer risk, mainly in never-smokers; no association with breast cancer except possibly in premenopausal women.

references.authors: Filippini T, Halldorsson TI, Capitão C, et al.
references.title: Dietary Acrylamide Exposure and Risk of Site-Specific Cancer: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Epidemiological Studies.
references.finding: No association between highest vs lowest dietary acrylamide exposure (median 23 µg/day) and any site-specific non-gynaecological cancer, except lung cancer in smokers.

references.authors: Hogervorst JG, Schouten LJ, Konings EJ, et al.
references.title: A prospective study of dietary acrylamide intake and the risk of endometrial, ovarian, and breast cancer.
references.finding: Top vs bottom quintile of acrylamide intake (40 vs 9 µg/day): ovarian cancer HR 1.78 and, in never-smokers, endometrial HR 1.99 and ovarian HR 2.22; no breast cancer association.

references.authors: Mucci LA, Dickman PW, Steineck G, et al.
references.title: Dietary acrylamide and cancer of the large bowel, kidney, and bladder: absence of an association in a population-based study in Sweden.
references.finding: No association between dietary acrylamide and cancers of the bowel, bladder or kidney; an unexpected inverse trend for large-bowel cancer.

references.authors: Olesen PT, Olsen A, Frandsen H, et al.
references.title: Acrylamide exposure and incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health Study.
references.n: Nested in Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort
references.finding: Acrylamide-haemoglobin adducts were not associated with breast cancer overall, but after smoking adjustment were associated with ER-positive breast cancer (IRR 2.7 per 10-fold increase).

references.authors: Obón-Santacana M, Lujan-Barroso L, Travis RC, et al.
references.title: Acrylamide and Glycidamide Hemoglobin Adducts and Epithelial Ovarian Cancer: A Nested Case-Control Study in Nonsmoking Postmenopausal Women from the EPIC Cohort.
references.finding: Acrylamide and glycidamide haemoglobin adducts showed no clear association with epithelial ovarian cancer and no dose-response.

references.authors: Pedersen M, von Stedingk H, Botsivali M, et al.
references.title: Birth weight, head circumference, and prenatal exposure to acrylamide from maternal diet: the European prospective mother-child study (NewGeneris).
references.finding: Highest vs lowest quartile of cord-blood acrylamide adducts was associated with 132 g lower birth weight and 0.33 cm smaller head circumference, also in non-smokers; fried potatoes predicted adducts.

references.authors: Wilson KM, Vesper HW, Tocco P, et al.
references.title: Validation of a food frequency questionnaire measurement of dietary acrylamide intake using hemoglobin adducts of acrylamide and glycidamide.
references.finding: FFQ-estimated acrylamide intake correlated only moderately (r = 0.31-0.34) with haemoglobin adducts of acrylamide and glycidamide, illustrating exposure misclassification in diet studies.

references.authors: Sansano M, Juan-Borrás M, Escriche I, et al.
references.title: Effect of pretreatments and air-frying, a novel technology, on acrylamide generation in fried potatoes.
references.finding: Air-frying potatoes at 180 °C produced about 90% less acrylamide than deep-oil frying; for deep frying, pretreatment soaks (citric acid, nicotinic acid, glycine 1%, NaCl 2%) cut acrylamide 80-90%.

references.authors: Yoon H, Jung MY, Choi SH, et al.
references.title: Effect of air-frying on formation and correlations of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, acrylamide, and heterocyclic aromatic amines in foods and risk assessment.
references.finding: In 184 air-fried foods, root and tuber crops had the most acrylamide and sea algae the most PAH4 and HCAs; margins of exposure for acrylamide suggested possible concern in some food groups.

references.authors: Uribarri J, Woodruff S, Goodman S, et al.
references.title: Advanced glycation end products in foods and a practical guide to their reduction in the diet.
references.finding: ELISA-based CML database of several hundred common foods: dry heat raises food AGEs 10-100-fold; moist heat, shorter cooking times, lower temperatures and acidic marinades reduce formation.

references.authors: Scheijen JLJM, Clevers E, Engelen L, et al.
references.title: Analysis of advanced glycation endproducts in selected food items by ultra-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry: Presentation of a dietary AGE database.
references.finding: UPLC-MS/MS database of CML, CEL and MG-H1 in 190 foods: highest in high-heat-processed nut and grain products and canned meats, lowest in fruit, vegetables, butter and coffee.

references.authors: Vlassara H, Cai W, Tripp E, et al.
references.title: Oral AGE restriction ameliorates insulin resistance in obese individuals with the metabolic syndrome: a randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: One year of a low-AGE diet lowered HOMA-IR from 3.1 to 1.9 and reduced AGEs, oxidative stress and inflammation, while the regular-AGE diet raised them (49 and 51 completers).

references.authors: Uribarri J, Cai W, Ramdas M, et al.
references.title: Restriction of advanced glycation end products improves insulin resistance in human type 2 diabetes: potential role of AGER1 and SIRT1.
references.finding: AGE restriction for 4 months lowered insulin, HOMA, TNF-alpha, serum AGEs and 8-isoprostanes in type 2 diabetes and normalised AGER1 and SIRT1.

references.authors: Semba RD, Gebauer SK, Baer DJ, et al.
references.title: Dietary intake of advanced glycation end products did not affect endothelial function and inflammation in healthy adults in a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Six weeks of a high- vs low-AGE diet (same foods, different cooking) had no effect on endothelial function (peripheral arterial tonometry) or inflammatory mediators.

references.authors: de Courten B, de Courten MP, Soldatos G, et al.
references.title: Diet low in advanced glycation end products increases insulin sensitivity in healthy overweight individuals: a double-blind, randomized, crossover trial.
references.finding: Double-blind crossover: 2 weeks of a low-AGE diet raised insulin sensitivity (clamp) by 1.3 mg/kg/min vs the high-AGE diet, without weight change.

references.authors: Kellow NJ, Savige GS
references.title: Dietary advanced glycation end-product restriction for the attenuation of insulin resistance, oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction: a systematic review.
references.finding: Some evidence that AGE restriction lowers HOMA-IR and AGE-LDL in type 2 diabetes, but 75% of trials lasted <6 weeks, over half were low quality, and evidence was low to very low.

references.authors: Clarke RE, Dordevic AL, Tan SM, et al.
references.title: Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Risk Factors for Chronic Disease: A Systematic Review of Randomised Controlled Trials.
references.finding: High-AGE diets increased circulating TNF-alpha and AGEs, and 8-isoprostanes in healthy adults; more high-quality trials needed.

references.authors: Baye E, de Courten MP, Walker K, et al.
references.title: Effect of dietary advanced glycation end products on inflammation and cardiovascular risks in healthy overweight adults: a randomised crossover trial.
references.finding: Two weeks of low vs high AGE diets did not change blood pressure, lipids or inflammatory markers (IL-6, MCP-1, TNF-alpha, CRP, NF-kB).

references.authors: Linkens AM, Houben AJ, Niessen PM, et al.
references.title: A 4-week high-AGE diet does not impair glucose metabolism and vascular function in obese individuals.
references.finding: Despite 2.7- to 5.3-fold differences in CML, CEL and MG-H1 intake, 4 weeks of low vs high AGE diets did not change insulin sensitivity, secretion, micro/macrovascular function, inflammation or lipids.

references.authors: Linkens AMA, Houben AJHM, Kroon AA, et al.
references.title: Habitual intake of dietary advanced glycation end products is not associated with generalized microvascular function-the Maastricht Study.
references.finding: Habitual intake of CML, CEL and MG-H1 (LC-MS/MS database) was not meaningfully associated with generalised microvascular function.

references.authors: Linkens AMA, Eussen SJMP, Houben AJHM, et al.
references.title: Habitual intake of advanced glycation endproducts is not associated with worse insulin sensitivity, worse beta cell function, or presence of prediabetes or type 2 diabetes: The Maastricht Study.
references.finding: Higher habitual dietary AGE intake was not associated with worse insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.

references.authors: Negrean M, Stirban A, Stratmann B, et al.
references.title: Effects of low- and high-advanced glycation endproduct meals on macro- and microvascular endothelial function and oxidative stress in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
references.finding: The same meal cooked to be high in AGEs reduced flow-mediated dilation by 36% vs 21% for the low-AGE version and raised oxidative stress markers.

references.authors: Jinno M, Takeuchi M, Watanabe A, et al.
references.title: Advanced glycation end-products accumulation compromises embryonic development and achievement of pregnancy by assisted reproductive technology.
references.finding: Higher serum toxic AGEs and follicular-fluid pentosidine correlated with fewer follicles, oocytes and embryos and lower ongoing pregnancy rates.

references.authors: Tantalaki E, Piperi C, Livadas S, et al.
references.title: Impact of dietary modification of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) on the hormonal and metabolic profile of women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
references.finding: A high-AGE diet raised serum AGEs, testosterone, insulin, HOMA-IR and oxidative stress compared with a low-AGE diet, without BMI change.

references.authors: Ramsden CE, Zamora D, Leelarthaepin B, et al.
references.title: Use of dietary linoleic acid for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease and death: evaluation of recovered data from the Sydney Diet Heart Study and updated meta-analysis.
references.n: 458 men after coronary event (Sydney Diet Heart Study)
references.finding: Replacing saturated fat with safflower oil/margarine raised all-cause (17.6% vs 11.8%, HR 1.62) and CHD death (HR 1.74); updated meta-analysis showed non-significant trends to harm.

references.authors: Ramsden CE, Zamora D, Majchrzak-Hong S, et al.
references.title: Re-evaluation of the traditional diet-heart hypothesis: analysis of recovered data from Minnesota Coronary Experiment (1968-73).
references.finding: A corn-oil diet lowered cholesterol 13.8% but gave no mortality benefit; each 30 mg/dL fall in cholesterol was associated with 22% higher death risk; meta-analysis of 5 RCTs showed no mortality benefit.

references.authors: Hooper L, Al-Khudairy L, Abdelhamid AS, et al.
references.title: Omega-6 fats for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
references.finding: Increasing omega-6 fats made little or no difference to all-cause mortality (RR 1.00) or CVD events (RR 0.97); may reduce myocardial infarction; low to very low quality evidence.

references.authors: Hooper L, Martin N, Jimoh OF, et al.
references.title: Reduction in saturated fat intake for cardiovascular disease.
references.finding: Reducing saturated fat lowered combined cardiovascular events by 17% (RR 0.83), more with greater cholesterol reduction; no clear difference between replacement by PUFA or carbohydrate.

references.authors: Marklund M, Wu JHY, Imamura F, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of Dietary Omega-6 Fatty Acids and Incident Cardiovascular Disease and Mortality.
references.finding: Higher blood/tissue linoleic acid was associated with lower total CVD (HR 0.93), CVD mortality (0.78) and ischaemic stroke (0.88); arachidonic acid was not associated with higher risk.

references.authors: Farvid MS, Ding M, Pan A, et al.
references.title: Dietary linoleic acid and risk of coronary heart disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest linoleic acid intake: 15% lower CHD events and 21% lower CHD deaths; 5% energy LA replacing saturated fat linked to 9% fewer events.

references.authors: Sacks FM, Lichtenstein AH, Wu JHY, et al.
references.title: Dietary Fats and Cardiovascular Disease: A Presidential Advisory From the American Heart Association.
references.finding: AHA Presidential Advisory: RCTs replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated vegetable oil reduced CVD by ~30%; recommends replacing saturated with unsaturated, especially polyunsaturated, fats.

references.authors: Johnson GH, Fritsche K
references.title: Effect of dietary linoleic acid on markers of inflammation in healthy persons: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Virtually no evidence from RCTs in healthy adults that adding linoleic acid raises inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-alpha, etc.).

references.authors: Li J, Guasch-Ferré M, Li Y, et al.
references.title: Dietary intake and biomarkers of linoleic acid and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest LA intake: total mortality RR 0.87, CVD mortality 0.87, cancer mortality 0.89; similar inverse associations for LA biomarkers.

references.authors: DiNicolantonio JJ, O'Keefe JH
references.title: Omega-6 vegetable oils as a driver of coronary heart disease: the oxidized linoleic acid hypothesis.
references.finding: Argues that oxidized linoleic acid in LDL drives coronary heart disease and that omega-6 vegetable oils should be limited; authors disclose commercial interests (books, nutraceutical company).

references.authors: Reaven P, Parthasarathy S, Grasse BJ, et al.
references.title: Effects of oleate-rich and linoleate-rich diets on the susceptibility of low density lipoprotein to oxidative modification in mildly hypercholesterolemic subjects.
references.finding: After 8 weeks, LDL from oleate-rich diets was less susceptible to copper-induced oxidation than LDL from linoleate-rich diets.

references.authors: Mozaffarian D, Micha R, Wallace S
references.title: Effects on coronary heart disease of increasing polyunsaturated fat in place of saturated fat: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Increasing PUFA (mostly LA) in place of saturated fat reduced CHD events by 19% (RR 0.81), about 10% per 5% energy.

references.authors: Hamley S
references.title: The effect of replacing saturated fat with mostly n-6 polyunsaturated fat on coronary heart disease: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
references.n: RCTs replacing SFA with n-6 PUFA
references.finding: In adequately controlled trials, replacing saturated fat with mostly n-6 PUFA did not reduce CHD events, CHD mortality or total mortality; benefits in earlier meta-analyses came from inadequately controlled trials.

references.authors: Ramsden CE, Ringel A, Feldstein AE, et al.
references.title: Lowering dietary linoleic acid reduces bioactive oxidized linoleic acid metabolites in humans.
references.finding: A 12-week low-LA diet reduced plasma oxidized linoleic acid metabolites (OXLAMs) and LA content of circulating lipid pools.

references.authors: Casal S, Malheiro R, Sendas A, et al.
references.title: Olive oil stability under deep-frying conditions.
references.finding: In domestic deep-frying, olive oils (including EVOO) lasted 24-27 h before reaching the 25% total polar compound legal limit vs 15 h for a vitamin-E-rich vegetable oil blend, which was far more susceptible to oxidation.

references.authors: Allouche Y, Jiménez A, Gaforio JJ, et al.
references.title: How heating affects extra virgin olive oil quality indexes and chemical composition.
references.finding: Heating EVOO at 180 °C for 36 h degraded tocopherols and polyphenols (cultivar-dependent), but oleic acid, sterols, squalene and triterpenes stayed stable; oil kept most minor compounds.

references.authors: Ramírez-Anaya Jdel P, Samaniego-Sánchez C, Castañeda-Saucedo MC, et al.
references.title: Phenols and the antioxidant capacity of Mediterranean vegetables prepared with extra virgin olive oil using different domestic cooking techniques.
references.finding: Cooking vegetables in EVOO (frying, sautéing) transferred olive phenols into the vegetables and kept or increased their phenolic content, while boiling reduced it.

references.authors: Qin P, Zhang M, Han M, et al.
references.title: Fried-food consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of observational studies.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest fried-food intake: major CVD RR 1.28, CHD 1.22, heart failure 1.37; no association with CVD or all-cause mortality; high heterogeneity.

references.authors: Sun Y, Liu B, Snetselaar LG, et al.
references.title: Association of fried food consumption with all cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality: prospective cohort study.
references.finding: At least one serving of fried food per day vs none: all-cause mortality HR 1.08; fried chicken ≥1/week HR 1.13 all-cause, 1.12 CVD mortality.

references.authors: Ng CY, Leong XF, Masbah N, et al.
references.title: Heated vegetable oils and cardiovascular disease risk factors.
references.finding: Repeatedly heated vegetable oils raise blood pressure, cholesterol and vascular inflammation in animal studies, attributed to lipid oxidation products.

references.authors: Guallar-Castillón P, Rodríguez-Artalejo F, Lopez-Garcia E, et al.
references.title: Consumption of fried foods and risk of coronary heart disease: Spanish cohort of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition study.
references.finding: No association between fried food intake and CHD (HR top vs bottom quarter 1.08) or all-cause mortality, whether olive or sunflower oil was used for frying.

references.authors: Cahill LE, Pan A, Chiuve SE, et al.
references.title: Fried-food consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease: a prospective study in 2 cohorts of US women and men.
references.finding: Fried food ≥7 times/week vs <1: type 2 diabetes RR 1.55 and CAD RR 1.21; associations largely attenuated after adjusting for BMI, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia.

references.authors: Choe E, Min DB
references.title: Chemistry of deep-fat frying oils.
references.finding: Deep-fat frying causes hydrolysis, oxidation and polymerisation; high temperature, number of fryings, free fatty acids, metals and unsaturation reduce oil stability.

references.authors: Grootveld M
references.title: Evidence-Based Challenges to the Continued Recommendation and Use of Peroxidatively-Susceptible Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid-Rich Culinary Oils for High-Temperature Frying Practises: Experimental Revelations Focused on Toxic Aldehydic Lipid Oxidation Products.
references.finding: Argues that PUFA-rich culinary oils generate the most toxic aldehydic lipid oxidation products during frying and calls for tolerable daily intakes and epidemiological studies of these compounds.

references.authors: Guillén MD, Uriarte PS
references.title: Contribution to further understanding of the evolution of sunflower oil submitted to frying temperature in a domestic fryer: study by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance.
references.finding: Sunflower oil held at 190 °C in a domestic fryer produced aldehydes very early, including genotoxic 4-hydroxy-trans-2-alkenals, well before reaching 25% polar compounds.

references.authors: Goicoechea E, Van Twillert K, Duits M, et al.
references.title: Use of an in vitro digestion model to study the bioaccessibility of 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal and related aldehydes present in oxidized oils rich in omega-6 acyl groups.
references.finding: In an in vitro digestion model, part of the toxic alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehydes (including 4-HNE) in oxidized omega-6-rich oils survived digestion and were bioaccessible.

references.authors: Ampem G, Le Gresley A, Grootveld M, et al.
references.title: High-resolution (1)H NMR analysis of continuous and discontinuous thermo-oxidative susceptibility of culinary oils during frying at 180 °C.
references.finding: NMR showed PUFA-rich culinary oils were the most susceptible to thermo-oxidation at 180 °C and coconut oil the most resistant; continuous heating caused more change than intermittent episodes.

references.authors: Sordini B, Urbani S, Selvaggini R, et al.
references.title: Evaluating the Effect of Packaging Materials on Extra Virgin Olive Oil Quality Under Simulated Household Use and Storage Conditions.
references.finding: Under simulated household use (25 °C, 12 h light, daily withdrawal over 40 days), EVOO in green PET bottles lost 44% of alpha-tocopherol and 26% of phenols and exceeded the legal peroxide limit after 30 days, vs 1-5% and 11-12% in bag-in-box or tin.

references.authors: Crupi P, Clodoveo ML, Desantis A, et al.
references.title: Effect of Long-Term Storage Temperature on the Quality of Extra-Virgin Olive Oil (Coratina cv.): A Multivariate Discriminant Approach.
references.finding: In 21 EVOOs stored in the dark for 18 months, peroxide values rose and polyphenols declined markedly after 6 months at room temperature, much less at 4 °C.

references.authors: Miglio C, Chiavaro E, Visconti A, et al.
references.title: Effects of different cooking methods on nutritional and physicochemical characteristics of selected vegetables.
references.finding: Boiling and steaming preserved carotenoids better than frying; frying retained fewer antioxidants; cooking softened the matrix and raised measured antioxidant capacity.

references.authors: Yuan GF, Sun B, Yuan J, et al.
references.title: Effects of different cooking methods on health-promoting compounds of broccoli.
references.finding: Steaming broccoli best retained vitamin C, chlorophyll and glucosinolates; stir-frying and stir-fry/boiling caused the largest losses.

references.authors: Song L, Thornalley PJ
references.title: Effect of storage, processing and cooking on glucosinolate content of Brassica vegetables.
references.finding: Steaming, microwaving and stir-frying did not significantly reduce Brassica glucosinolates, whereas boiling leached ~90% of losses into the water; fine shredding then standing lost up to 75% in 6 h.

references.authors: Palermo M, Pellegrini N, Fogliano V
references.title: The effect of cooking on the phytochemical content of vegetables.
references.finding: Steaming generally preserves phenols and glucosinolates best; carotenoids often become more extractable after more severe heating.

references.authors: Dewanto V, Wu X, Adom KK, et al.
references.title: Thermal processing enhances the nutritional value of tomatoes by increasing total antioxidant activity.
references.finding: Heating tomatoes at 88 °C for 2-30 min raised bioaccessible lycopene and total antioxidant activity while vitamin C fell.

references.authors: Conaway CC, Getahun SM, Liebes LL, et al.
references.title: Disposition of glucosinolates and sulforaphane in humans after ingestion of steamed and fresh broccoli.
references.finding: Isothiocyanate bioavailability was ~3 times higher from fresh broccoli (32%) than steamed broccoli in which myrosinase was inactivated (10%).

references.authors: Lee S, Choi Y, Jeong HS, et al.
references.title: Effect of different cooking methods on the content of vitamins and true retention in selected vegetables.
references.finding: Vitamin C retention in cooked vegetables ranged from 0 to 91%, generally highest after microwaving and lowest after boiling.

references.authors: Alves C, Saleh A, Alaofè H
references.title: Iron-containing cookware for the reduction of iron deficiency anemia among children and females of reproductive age in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review.
references.finding: Iron pots or ingots raised haemoglobin or iron indices in about half of studies, mainly in children; compliance varied and safety data are limited.

references.authors: Sajid M, Ilyas M
references.title: PTFE-coated non-stick cookware and toxicity concerns: a perspective.
references.finding: PTFE-coated non-stick pans can release gases and chemicals when overheated; PFOA (now replaced by GenX and others) has been detected in emissions; human toxicity data are limited.

references.authors: Albert BB, Derraik JG, Cameron-Smith D, et al.
references.title: Fish oil supplements in New Zealand are highly oxidised and do not meet label content of n-3 PUFA.
references.finding: Of 32 New Zealand fish-oil supplements, 83% exceeded the recommended peroxide value, 25% anisidine value and 50% TOTOX; only 8% met all limits and most contained <67% of labelled EPA+DHA.

references.authors: Jackowski SA, Alvi AZ, Mirajkar A, et al.
references.title: Oxidation levels of North American over-the-counter n-3 (omega-3) supplements and the influence of supplement formulation and delivery form on evaluating oxidative safety.
references.finding: Of 171 North American omega-3 supplements, 50% exceeded voluntary oxidation limits; flavoured products, bulk oils and children's products were more oxidized than plain capsules; most authors were affiliated with an omega-3 company.

references.authors: Bannenberg G, Mallon C, Edwards H, et al.
references.title: Omega-3 Long-Chain Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Content and Oxidation State of Fish Oil Supplements in New Zealand.
references.finding: Industry-association (GOED) testing of 47 New Zealand fish-oil products found 72-86% compliant with voluntary oxidation limits and 91% meeting EPA/DHA label claims, contradicting Albert 2015.

references.authors: Ottestad I, Vogt G, Retterstøl K, et al.
references.title: Oxidised fish oil does not influence established markers of oxidative stress in healthy human subjects: a randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: 7 weeks of 8 g/day oxidized fish oil (1.6 g EPA+DHA) did not change urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha, plasma HNE/HHE, hs-CRP or antioxidant enzymes vs fresh fish oil or high-oleic sunflower oil.

references.authors: Rundblad A, Holven KB, Ottestad I, et al.
references.title: High-quality fish oil has a more favourable effect than oxidised fish oil on intermediate-density lipoprotein and LDL subclasses: a randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: High-quality fish oil (PV 4) lowered IDL and LDL particle subclasses compared with oxidized fish oil (PV 18, AV 9) and high-oleic sunflower oil.

references.authors: García-Hernández VM, Gallar M, Sánchez-Soriano J, et al.
references.title: Effect of omega-3 dietary supplements with different oxidation levels in the lipidic profile of women: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Less-oxidized omega-3 capsules lowered triglycerides and cholesterol over 30 days, whereas highly oxidized capsules worsened cholesterol.

references.authors: Mason RP, Sherratt SCR
references.title: Omega-3 fatty acid fish oil dietary supplements contain saturated fats and oxidized lipids that may interfere with their intended biological benefits.
references.finding: Three top-selling US fish-oil supplements exceeded oxidation limits (a prescription product did not), and omega-3 isolated from them failed to inhibit small dense LDL oxidation in vitro.

references.authors: Gooley JJ, Chamberlain K, Smith KA, et al.
references.title: Exposure to room light before bedtime suppresses melatonin onset and shortens melatonin duration in humans.
references.finding: Room light (<200 lux) before bedtime vs dim light delayed melatonin onset in 99% and shortened melatonin duration by ~90 min; room light during sleep hours suppressed melatonin >50% in 85% of trials.

references.authors: Chang AM, Aeschbach D, Duffy JF, et al.
references.title: Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Reading a light-emitting e-reader for ~4 h before bed for 5 nights, vs a printed book, lengthened sleep onset, suppressed melatonin, delayed the circadian clock and reduced next-morning alertness.

references.authors: Zeitzer JM
references.title: Real life trumps laboratory in matters of public health.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Letter arguing that the e-reader laboratory findings may not translate to real-life public-health relevance.

references.authors: Chang AM, Czeisler CA
references.title: Reply to Zeitzer: Good science, in or out of the laboratory, should prevail.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Authors' reply defending the controlled laboratory design and its relevance to everyday evening device use.

references.authors: Phillips AJK, Vidafar P, Burns AC, et al.
references.title: High sensitivity and interindividual variability in the response of the human circadian system to evening light.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Half-maximal melatonin suppression occurred at only ~25 lux of evening light; 10, 30 and 50 lux delayed melatonin onset by 22, 77 and 109 min; individual sensitivity varied over 10-fold.

references.authors: Brown TM, Brainard GC, Cajochen C, et al.
references.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults.
references.finding: Expert consensus: daytime light ≥250 lux melanopic EDI at the eye; ≤10 lux melanopic EDI in the 3 h before bed; ≤1 lux melanopic EDI in the sleep environment (≤10 if some light is needed).

references.authors: Wright KP Jr, McHill AW, Birks BR, et al.
references.title: Entrainment of the human circadian clock to the natural light-dark cycle.
references.finding: A week of camping with natural light only advanced the circadian clock (melatonin onset moved toward sunset) and reduced differences between late and early chronotypes.

references.authors: Stothard ER, McHill AW, Depner CM, et al.
references.title: Circadian Entrainment to the Natural Light-Dark Cycle across Seasons and the Weekend.
references.finding: A summer weekend of camping achieved ~69% of the circadian advance of a full week; the biological night expanded in winter natural light.

references.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Rutter MK, et al.
references.title: Personal light exposure patterns and incidence of type 2 diabetes: analysis of 13 million hours of light sensor data and 670,000 person-years of prospective observation.
references.finding: Brighter night-light exposure was associated with higher type 2 diabetes risk (HR 1.29, 1.39 and 1.53 for 50-70th, 70-90th and 90-100th percentiles vs darkest nights); authors disclose lighting-industry funding.

references.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al.
references.title: Brighter nights and darker days predict higher mortality risk: A prospective analysis of personal light exposure in >88,000 individuals.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Brighter day light was associated with lower all-cause mortality (aHR ~0.66-0.83 for top decile) and brighter night light with higher mortality (aHR 1.21-1.34 top decile) over 8 years.

references.authors: Mason IC, Grimaldi D, Reid KJ, et al.
references.title: Light exposure during sleep impairs cardiometabolic function.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: One night of sleeping in 100 lux room light vs <3 lux raised night-time heart rate, lowered heart rate variability and increased next-morning insulin resistance.

references.authors: Park YM, White AJ, Jackson CL, et al.
references.title: Association of Exposure to Artificial Light at Night While Sleeping With Risk of Obesity in Women.
references.finding: Sleeping with a TV or light on was associated with gaining ≥5 kg (RR 1.17) and incident obesity (RR 1.33) over ~5.7 years.

references.authors: Obayashi K, Saeki K, Iwamoto J, et al.
references.title: Exposure to light at night, nocturnal urinary melatonin excretion, and obesity/dyslipidemia in the elderly: a cross-sectional analysis of the HEIJO-KYO study.
references.finding: Bedroom light ≥3 lux at night was associated with higher odds of obesity (OR 1.89) and dyslipidaemia (OR 1.72), independent of urinary melatonin.

references.authors: Singh S, Keller PR, Busija L, et al.
references.title: Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults.
references.finding: Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses probably do not reduce eye strain; effects on sleep quality were indeterminate with mixed results and high risk of bias.

references.authors: Duraccio KM, Zaugg KK, Blackburn RC, et al.
references.title: Does iPhone night shift mitigate negative effects of smartphone use on sleep outcomes in emerging adults?
references.finding: iPhone Night Shift mode did not improve sleep outcomes vs normal phone use; among those sleeping >6.8 h, no phone before bed gave the best sleep.

references.authors: Schöllhorn I, Stefani O, Lucas RJ, et al.
references.title: Melanopic irradiance defines the impact of evening display light on sleep latency, melatonin and alertness.
references.finding: At equal screen brightness, low-melanopic display light shortened sleep latency, reduced melatonin suppression and advanced melatonin onset vs high-melanopic light, dose-dependently.

references.authors: van Maanen A, Meijer AM, van der Heijden KB, et al.
references.title: The effects of light therapy on sleep problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Light therapy improved sleep problems overall (g 0.39), circadian rhythm sleep disorders (g 0.41) and insomnia (g 0.47); effects small to medium, smaller in RCTs, with publication bias.

references.authors: Figueiro MG, Steverson B, Heerwagen J, et al.
references.title: The impact of daytime light exposures on sleep and mood in office workers.
references.finding: High morning circadian-effective light was associated with shorter sleep onset latency, better sleep quality and stronger circadian entrainment, especially in winter.

references.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al.
references.title: Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study.
references.finding: More regular sleep (Sleep Regularity Index) was associated with 20-48% lower all-cause and 22-57% lower cardiometabolic mortality vs the least regular quintile; regularity predicted mortality better than duration.

references.authors: Wong PM, Hasler BP, Kamarck TW, et al.
references.title: Social Jetlag, Chronotype, and Cardiometabolic Risk.
references.finding: Greater social jetlag was associated with lower HDL, higher triglycerides, insulin resistance and adiposity, independent of sleep duration and quality.

references.authors: Knutson KL, von Schantz M
references.title: Associations between chronotype, morbidity and mortality in the UK Biobank cohort.
references.finding: Definite evening types had 10% higher all-cause mortality than definite morning types (HR 1.10) over 6.5 years.

references.authors: Garaulet M, Gómez-Abellán P, Alburquerque-Béjar JJ, et al.
references.title: Timing of food intake predicts weight loss effectiveness.
references.finding: Late lunch eaters (after 15:00) lost less weight over 20 weeks than early eaters despite similar energy intake, expenditure and sleep.

references.authors: Lopez-Minguez J, Saxena R, Bandín C, et al.
references.title: Late dinner impairs glucose tolerance in MTNR1B risk allele carriers: A randomized, cross-over study.
references.finding: Eating dinner late, when melatonin is high, impaired glucose tolerance, significantly so only in MTNR1B risk-allele carriers.

references.authors: Garaulet M, Lopez-Minguez J, Dashti HS, et al.
references.title: Interplay of Dinner Timing and MTNR1B Type 2 Diabetes Risk Variant on Glucose Tolerance and Insulin Secretion: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
references.finding: An evening glucose load 1 h before habitual bedtime vs 4 h before gave 3.5-fold higher melatonin, 6.7% lower insulin AUC and 8.3% higher glucose AUC, worse in MTNR1B G-allele carriers.

references.authors: Gu C, Brereton N, Schweitzer A, et al.
references.title: Metabolic Effects of Late Dinner in Healthy Volunteers-A Randomized Crossover Clinical Trial.
references.finding: Dinner at 22:00 vs 18:00 raised nocturnal glucose, delayed the triglyceride peak and reduced fatty acid oxidation, especially in habitually early sleepers; sleep architecture unchanged.

references.authors: Jakubowicz D, Barnea M, Wainstein J, et al.
references.title: High caloric intake at breakfast vs. dinner differentially influences weight loss of overweight and obese women.
references.finding: On a 1,400 kcal diet, a 700 kcal breakfast/200 kcal dinner pattern produced more weight and waist loss and larger falls in glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR and triglycerides than the reverse.

references.authors: Vujović N, Piron MJ, Qian J, et al.
references.title: Late isocaloric eating increases hunger, decreases energy expenditure, and modifies metabolic pathways in adults with overweight and obesity.
references.finding: Under tightly controlled conditions, isocaloric late eating increased hunger and ghrelin:leptin ratio and decreased waketime energy expenditure and core temperature.

references.authors: Ruddick-Collins LC, Morgan PJ, Fyfe CL, et al.
references.title: Timing of daily calorie loading affects appetite and hunger responses without changes in energy metabolism in healthy subjects with obesity.
references.finding: Morning- vs evening-loaded calorie distribution for 4 weeks did not change energy expenditure or weight loss; morning loading reduced hunger.

references.authors: Leung GKW, Huggins CE, Ware RS, et al.
references.title: Time of day difference in postprandial glucose and insulin responses: Systematic review and meta-analysis of acute postprandial studies.
references.finding: Postprandial glucose after an identical meal was lower in the day than at night (SMD -1.66), consistent with poorer glucose tolerance at night.

references.authors: Dashti HS, Gómez-Abellán P, Qian J, et al.
references.title: Late eating is associated with cardiometabolic risk traits, obesogenic behaviors, and impaired weight loss.
references.finding: Late eaters had higher BMI, triglycerides and lower insulin sensitivity at baseline and lost ~80 g/week less weight than early eaters.

references.authors: Young IE, Poobalan A, Steinbeck K, et al.
references.title: Distribution of energy intake across the day and weight loss: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: In energy-reduced diets, shifting intake earlier gave 1.23 kg more weight loss and improvements in HOMA-IR, fasting glucose and LDL.

references.authors: Fong M, Caterson ID, Madigan CD
references.title: Are large dinners associated with excess weight, and does eating a smaller dinner achieve greater weight loss? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Observational links between large evening intake and BMI were inconsistent and trials showed no significant difference in weight change between small and large dinners.

references.authors: Sutton EF, Beyl R, Early KS, et al.
references.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves Insulin Sensitivity, Blood Pressure, and Oxidative Stress Even without Weight Loss in Men with Prediabetes.
references.finding: Early time-restricted feeding (6 h window, dinner before 15:00) for 5 weeks improved insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and oxidative stress (8-isoprostane) without weight loss.

references.authors: Peters B, Schwarz J, Schuppelius B, et al.
references.title: Intended isocaloric time-restricted eating shifts circadian clocks but does not improve cardiometabolic health in women with overweight.
references.finding: Two weeks of early (8:00-16:00) or late (13:00-21:00) isocaloric time-restricted eating did not improve insulin sensitivity or glucose, lipid, inflammatory or oxidative stress markers, despite shifting circadian phase.

references.authors: Scheer FA, Hilton MF, Mantzoros CS, et al.
references.title: Adverse metabolic and cardiovascular consequences of circadian misalignment.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Eating and sleeping ~12 h out of phase lowered leptin 17%, raised glucose 6% despite 22% more insulin, reversed the cortisol rhythm and raised blood pressure; 3 of 8 had prediabetic postprandial glucose.

references.authors: Morris CJ, Yang JN, Garcia JI, et al.
references.title: Endogenous circadian system and circadian misalignment impact glucose tolerance via separate mechanisms in humans.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Postprandial glucose was 17% higher in the biological evening than morning, and circadian misalignment itself raised it a further 6%, via reduced insulin sensitivity.

references.authors: Morris CJ, Purvis TE, Hu K, et al.
references.title: Circadian misalignment increases cardiovascular disease risk factors in humans.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Three days of circadian misalignment raised 24-h blood pressure (+3.0/1.5 mmHg) and IL-6, CRP, resistin and TNF-alpha by 3-29%.

references.authors: Buxton OM, Cain SW, O'Connor SP, et al.
references.title: Adverse metabolic consequences in humans of prolonged sleep restriction combined with circadian disruption.
references.finding: Three weeks of sleep restriction (5.6 h/24 h) combined with 28-h days lowered resting metabolic rate and raised postprandial glucose through inadequate insulin secretion; reversed with recovery.

references.authors: Teixeira KRC, Dos Santos CP, de Medeiros LA, et al.
references.title: Night workers have lower levels of antioxidant defenses and higher levels of oxidative stress damage when compared to day workers.
references.finding: Night workers had higher TBARS and hydrogen peroxide and lower total antioxidant capacity, catalase and SOD than day workers; social jetlag was not associated with these markers.

references.authors: Bhatti P, Mirick DK, Randolph TW, et al.
references.title: Oxidative DNA damage during sleep periods among nightshift workers.
references.finding: Night-shift workers excreted less urinary 8-OH-dG during day sleep than day workers during night sleep, interpreted as reduced oxidative DNA repair linked to melatonin disruption.

references.authors: Bhatti P, Mirick DK, Randolph TW, et al.
references.title: Oxidative DNA damage during night shift work.
references.finding: Melatonin was much lower during night work than night sleep, and urinary 8-OH-dG during night work was only 20% of night-sleep levels, interpreted as reduced repair.

references.authors: Zanif U, Lai AS, Parks J, et al.
references.title: Melatonin supplementation and oxidative DNA damage repair capacity among night shift workers: a randomised placebo-controlled trial.
references.finding: Melatonin before day sleep for 4 weeks gave a borderline 1.8-fold increase in urinary 8-OH-dG during day sleep (p = 0.06), interpreted as better repair capacity; no change during night work.

references.authors: Jiang Z, Dou Y, Lei Y, et al.
references.title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Unravels the Potential Molecular Link Between Night Shift Work-Related Circadian Disruption and Elevated Blood Pressure in Human and Mouse Models.
references.finding: Simulated night-shift work in mice raised blood pressure with clock-gene disruption, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress; in human night workers exposure duration tracked blood pressure and mitochondrial markers.

references.authors: IARC Monographs Vol 124 group
references.title: Carcinogenicity of night shift work.
references.finding: IARC Monograph 124 classified night shift work as probably carcinogenic to humans (Group 2A), based on limited human evidence and sufficient animal evidence.

references.authors: Vetter C, Devore EE, Wegrzyn LR, et al.
references.title: Association Between Rotating Night Shift Work and Risk of Coronary Heart Disease Among Women.
references.finding: Longer duration of rotating night-shift work was associated with a statistically significant but small absolute increase in CHD risk, which waned after stopping shift work.

references.authors: Gan Y, Yang C, Tong X, et al.
references.title: Shift work and diabetes mellitus: a meta-analysis of observational studies.
references.finding: Ever shift work was associated with 9% higher diabetes risk (OR 1.09), higher in men (1.37) and rotating shifts.

references.authors: Gao Y, Gan T, Jiang L, et al.
references.title: Association between shift work and risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of observational studies.
references.finding: Shift work was associated with higher type 2 diabetes risk (~10%), especially night and rotating shifts, with possible dose-response with years of exposure in women.

references.authors: Torquati L, Mielke GI, Brown WJ, et al.
references.title: Shift work and the risk of cardiovascular disease. A systematic review and meta-analysis including dose-response relationship.
references.finding: Shift workers had 17% higher risk of any CVD event and 26% higher CHD morbidity; risk rose 7.1% per additional 5 years after the first 5 years.

references.authors: Travis RC, Balkwill A, Fensom GK, et al.
references.title: Night Shift Work and Breast Cancer Incidence: Three Prospective Studies and Meta-analysis of Published Studies.
references.finding: Night shift work was not associated with breast cancer (RR 0.99), even after 20 or 30+ years.

references.authors: Stocker LJ, Macklon NS, Cheong YC, et al.
references.title: Influence of shift work on early reproductive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Shift work was associated with menstrual disruption (aOR 1.15) and infertility (OR 1.80, I² 94%); night shifts with early pregnancy loss (OR 1.29).

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Rich-Edwards JW, Lawson CC, et al.
references.title: Work schedule and physical factors in relation to fecundity in nurses.
references.finding: No shift-work pattern was associated with time to pregnancy; working >40 h/week and heavy lifting were.

references.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Souter I, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Occupational factors and markers of ovarian reserve and response among women at a fertility centre.
references.n: 313-473 women at a fertility centre (EARTH study)
references.finding: Women working evening/night/rotating shifts had 2.3 fewer mature oocytes retrieved after ovarian stimulation than day workers.

references.authors: Wang Y, He M, Ling X, et al.
references.title: Rotating shiftwork in men is linked to decreased fecundity, attributable primarily to sperm concentration and vitality: 24-month follow-up in 3425 males of PREBIC cohort.
references.finding: Rotating shift workers had 16% lower hazard of pregnancy within 1 year and ~11% lower sperm concentration and total count; fixed shift workers did not differ from day workers.

references.authors: Boeri L, Passarelli F, Basadonna LM, et al.
references.title: Oxidative Stress and Semen Quality Among Night- and Day-Shift Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study.
references.finding: Night-shift work independently predicted elevated oxidative stress (d-ROMs, OR 2.1); in an uncontrolled subgroup, antioxidant supplementation lowered d-ROMs more in night workers.

references.authors: Green A, Barak S, Shine L, et al.
references.title: Exposure by males to light emitted from media devices at night is linked with decline of sperm quality and correlated with sleep quality measures.
references.finding: Evening and post-bedtime smartphone/tablet use correlated negatively with sperm motility, progressive motility and concentration.

references.authors: Tian R, Yang T, Xiao C, et al.
references.title: Outdoor artificial light at night and male sperm quality: A retrospective cohort study in China.
references.finding: Each 100 nW/cm²/sr higher outdoor artificial light at night was associated with lower sperm motility, most strongly in men under 25.

references.authors: Reiter RJ, Tamura H, Tan DX, et al.
references.title: Melatonin and the circadian system: contributions to successful female reproduction.
references.finding: Follicular fluid melatonin exceeds blood levels and protects the oocyte from oxidative stress around ovulation; light at night suppresses melatonin and should be avoided.
